title: Fresh eyes

story: RH-1234's code is written and its three checks pass. A reviewer that has never seen Nova's reasoning reads the diff and reports three important problems. One of them: while the table is loading, the empty card flashes for one render. Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, fixes all three, and the reviewer runs again.

In the second round the same problem is back, now at line 35 instead of line 31. Nova fixes it again. In the third round it is at line 38, then at line 41. After an hour the receipt says "fixed 8 findings", which sounds great, but the card still flashes, and the real story, that Nova and the reviewer disagree about how loading should work, is hidden under eight green ticks. Nobody wants a round limit that cuts the work in half. Nobody wants a loop that goes in circles either.
hook.question: How does the review loop know when it is done, without a round limit and without going in circles?

p: After the build, three helpers check Nova's work, and each one is a separate session started by the harness, so none of them sees Nova's transcript or notes. You met that idea in the lesson on judges: a reader who never saw the reasoning cannot be talked into agreeing with it. What differs between the three is the slice of the work each one gets.

The self-reviewer gets the ticket, the approved plan and the diff, and reads the repo with Read, Grep and Glob only. It looks through the same lenses Byte, our review agent, uses (correctness, security, conventions, performance), and marks each finding important or nit. Important means a bug, a security problem, a requirement or plan item that is missing, or a change the plan did not ask for; everything else is a nit, counted but not fixed one by one. The scope judge gets less: only the ticket and the diff, and it can veto unrelated changes and weakened tests. The QA agent gets no code at all: only the QA plan and the running app in a browser, where it tries each check like a tester and records a short video.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the QA agent in a browser
p: The QA agent runs on FCP Lab, the full product on the VM with fake seed data, and drives a browser through a pinned Playwright MCP server, one fresh browser context per check, with video on. Layout checks run at 760 and 1440 pixels wide, the two widths the frontend promises. Its tools are the browser and reading its own folder of instructions; it may not read the checkout, and that deny rule needs the absolute form with two slashes, Read(//work/fcp/**), because a single slash is read relative to the session's folder. Testers can be too kind, so before the pilot it is calibrated on eight to ten planted bugs, such as a toast that says saved while the form is still saving, an empty state that overlaps the table at 760, or a count that is off by one, and it must fail every one. Its results go to .nova/qa_results.json, and Nova cannot mark a failed check as passed: a fail comes back to Nova as a finding.

One review pass leaves things behind, because fixes create new code to review. So the self-review is a loop. A fresh reviewer session reads the diff and returns its findings. For each important one, Nova either fixes it or answers with a reason, because the reviewer can be wrong too. Then the harness runs the QA checks again, since a fix must never quietly break a check the requester approved. Then a new reviewer session reads the new diff, and the loop goes round.

The loop has no round limit, on purpose. A limit of three rounds would stop a run that is one fix away from clean, and it would protect nothing: a long loop costs money, but it cannot push to main or leak a key. Instead the loop ends on a condition: nothing important is open, or every open item is with a person. The progress watcher, which reads every tool call, still notices a run that stops making progress. Once the reviewer is clean, the scope judge reads the final diff once; on a veto Nova reverts the unrelated change or explains why the ticket needs it, and a second veto on the same item goes to a person.

The condition only works if the loop can recognise a finding it has seen before, and the hook shows why that is hard: the flashing card came back at line 35, then 38, then 41, because each fix moved the code. So every finding gets a fingerprint, a short hash of what the finding is about: the file, the rule and the message, with numbers and extra spaces removed. The line number is left out on purpose, because it changes every time the code above it changes, while the problem stays the same.

Now the loop can tell real progress from ping-pong, two sides undoing each other round after round. A finding whose fingerprint is new is work to do. A finding whose fingerprint was already fixed once and is back means the fix did not hold, or Nova and the reviewer disagree. Fixing it a second time would only repeat the argument, so the loop stops working on it, asks the requester in the ticket's Slack thread, and lists it as left. Everything ends in a receipt, one line for the people who come next: "Found 6 · fixed 5 · left 1, because it came back after a fix". It goes into the PR description, and Byte reads it too, so Byte does not report the same problems again.

notes.text: Normalise first: lower case, every number becomes #, spaces collapse. "line 31" and "line 35" become the same text.
File, rule and message. Not the line: it moves with every fix while the problem stays.
A finding already left with a person is not counted again, so the loop can end.
The end condition: no important finding is open. No round counter anywhere.
Fixed before and back again: ping-pong. Stop and ask a person instead of a second fix.
Every round ends with the QA checks, so a fix cannot quietly break one.

lab.title: A review loop that ends
lab.goal: Run a self-review loop on recorded reviewer rounds, see fingerprints turn a returning finding into a question for a person, and break the fingerprint to watch the loop go in circles.

guess.q: Round 1: the reviewer reports "the empty card flashes while loading (line 31)" and Nova fixes it. Round 2: the same message, now at line 35. The fingerprint uses the file, the rule and the message with numbers removed. What does the loop do?

options.text: Fixes it again: line 35 is a new finding.
options.why: Without the line, both findings have the same fingerprint. The loop sees that it was fixed once already.

options.text: Stops working on it, asks the requester, and lists it as left on the receipt.
options.why: A fixed finding that comes back is ping-pong. A second fix would repeat the same argument, so a person decides.

options.text: Stops the whole run with an error.
options.why: One returning finding does not end the run. The loop goes on with the other findings, and this one waits for a person.

follow.say: Make a folder. This lab needs only Node, no packages.
Save four recorded reviewer rounds for RH-1234. Each round is what a fresh reviewer session reported. Notice the loading finding: it comes back in every round, at a new line each time.
Write the loop. Fixing is simulated (every finding counts as fixed), so you can watch the fingerprints and the end condition alone.

lab.build: Nova does not have to agree with every finding. Add a fifth finding to round 1 of rounds.json: the performance rule, ProjectsTable.tsx line 60, "Filtering 1,000 projects on every key press may be slow", important, with an extra field disagree: "filtering 1,000 names takes well under a millisecond". Then change the loop so a finding with a disagree field is left with that reason instead of fixed, and printed as a left line. Run it: the receipt now lists two items left, each with its reason.

lab.fix: Someone made the fingerprint "more precise": it now includes the line, f.path:f.line, and normalise only trims the text. This morning a run spent an hour fixing the same loading problem four times, and its PR proudly said fixed 8 while the card still flashed. Make that change in a copy, run it to see Found 8 · fixed 8 · left 0 and rounds 3 and 4 running, then explain which part of the fingerprint broke the loop and repair it.
explain: Why does the fingerprint leave out the line number?
A finding was fixed in round 1 and is back in round 2. Why is a person a better answer than a second fix?
Why does the loop end on "nothing important is open" instead of after a fixed number of rounds?
lab.done: The loop ends after two rounds with one item left for a person, and you can show how one extra field in the fingerprint turns it into a loop that goes in circles.

check.q: Why does a finding's fingerprint leave out the line number?

options.text: Because reviewers often get line numbers wrong
options.why: The line can be exactly right and still be useless: it moves every time the code above it changes.

options.text: Because a fix moves the code, so the same problem shows up at a new line and must still be recognised
options.why: File, rule and normalised message stay the same while the problem stays. The line does not.
Hash length has nothing to do with what goes in. The point is what should count as the same finding.

check.q: The self-review loop has run five rounds on a big ticket, and every round brings new, real findings that Nova fixes. What should happen?

options.text: Stop after five rounds; that is enough review
options.why: A round limit would cut the run in the middle while it is still making progress, and it protects nothing a wall does not already protect.

options.text: Hand the ticket back to the requester
options.why: Real findings being fixed is progress, not a reason to give up.

options.text: Keep going: the loop ends when nothing important is open, and the progress watcher acts only if the run stops making progress
options.why: The end is a condition, not a count. Fingerprints stop the circles; new findings are real work.

check.q: Which reader gets the least of Nova's work, and why is that useful?

options.text: The scope judge: only the ticket and the diff, so it judges every change by the ticket alone
options.why: Without the plan or Nova's notes, it cannot be persuaded that a "while I was here" change was needed. Its question is simple: does each change serve the ticket?
The self-reviewer also gets the ticket and the approved plan, because it checks that every plan item is done.

options.text: The QA agent: only Nova's notes
options.why: The QA agent never reads Nova's notes or the code. It gets the QA plan and the running app.

p: The self-reviewer is reviewOnce() in harness/src/review.ts: its own query() session on Opus 5.5 at medium, settingSources ["project"] so frontend/AGENTS.md applies, allowedTools Read, Grep and Glob with Bash, Edit and Write disallowed (git diff --no-index or --output= could read or write outside the repo), permissionMode dontAsk, and Byte's lens files from /opt/ai-agents/byte-playbooks. The harness writes the diff to /run/nova/review/diff.patch itself. Each finding gets a sha1 fingerprint and is appended to .nova/review.jsonl; selfReview() in harness/src/self-review.ts runs the loop, uses the review panel workflow instead of a single reviewer when the plan asks for one, and writes .nova/receipt.json for the PR body and for Byte.

The scope judge is harness/src/judges/scope.ts on Sonnet 5.5 at medium with tools: [] and settingSources: [], and it also receives a mechanical list of test changes (removed assertions, .skip and .only, longer timeouts). Before it is trusted it is checked against people's labels on 20 bench diffs plus 10 with a planted unrelated refactor or loosened assertion. The QA agent's qaOptions() in harness/src/qa.ts must use Read(//work/fcp/**) and mcp__playwright__* in its rules (the sketch has a single slash and mcp__playwright), and every judge's schema needs target: "draft-7".

tickets.why: The loop itself: review, fix, recheck, fingerprints for ping-pong, and the receipt.
The fresh-context self-reviewer with Byte's lenses and read-only tools.
The scope judge that sees only the ticket and the diff, and can veto.
The QA agent that runs the QA plan in a browser, with a video per check.

words.plain: A fresh session that reads the ticket, the approved plan and the diff, and reports findings without editing.
A judge that sees only the ticket and the diff and can veto changes the ticket did not ask for.
A short hash of a finding's file, rule and normalised message, without the line, so a returning finding is recognised.
The same finding fixed and reported again and again, because two sides disagree.
One line for the PR and Byte: found, fixed, and left with a reason.

review.q: From memory: what each of the three readers gets, and what it may touch.
review.a: Self-reviewer: ticket, approved plan, diff; Read, Grep, Glob only. Scope judge: ticket and diff only; no tools. QA agent: QA plan and the running app in a browser; no code, no diff.

review.q: A teammate proposes "max 3 review rounds" to save money. What do you answer?
review.a: A round limit cuts a run that is still making progress and protects nothing. The loop ends when nothing important is open; fingerprints stop ping-pong by sending a returning finding to a person; the progress watcher catches a run that stops moving.

review.q: What is the receipt for, and who reads it?
review.a: It tells the next readers what was already looked at: found, fixed, and left with reasons. It goes into the PR description for people, and Byte reads it so it does not repeat the same findings.

remember: Fresh readers each see a slice; the loop goes round until nothing important is open, and a finding that comes back after a fix goes to a person, not round again.
